newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hot, dry weather threatens SAfrica 97/98 maize crop.
newsitem.headline: Hot, dry weather threatens SAfrica 97/98 maize crop.

text.p: Hopes of another bumper South African maize crop this year may be dashed if the hot and dry weather, which has already damaged plants in the eastern parts of the country, persists in the next six weeks.

The National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said on Friday current estimates for the 1997/98 crop, which will be harvested from May, are at around nine million tonnes -- down from nearly 10 million tonnes in the 1996/97 season.

But Kit Le Clus, Nampo's research and development manager, told Reuters estimates could drop well below nine million tonnes, shrinking the country's potential for exports of its most important crop, if rainfall remained scarce.

"It is now the most moisture critical time in the plant's life...The current situation is that in the last three weeks we have had extremely hot, dry weather and that has definitely damaged the crops," Le Clus said.

He, however, cautioned that Nampo's estimate of nine million was "only a guess" as it was difficult to gauge the size of the crop at this stage. The National Crop Estimates Committee said an official acreage estimate would be released next Friday and the first crop estimate around March 20.

Le Clus said weather forecasts predicted only light rain for the rest of this month and below average precipitation in March. "That is disconcerting and if it comes through then we are going to have significantly more crop damage...At this stage it is not sure whether we will have surplus maize," he said.

Drought fears have already spread through the market boosting trading volumes in maize futures contracts on the South African Futures Exchange (Safex) this month as players search for ways to hedge crop risk.
"We have seen a very nice upturn in volumes," Rod Blondin, Safex's general manager told Reuters this week, adding that a record 422 yellow and white maize contracts had traded last Friday.
This compared with on average around 15 trades a day in the third quarter of last year, and 25 a day in the fourth quarter.
White maize futures for March delivery were last bid at 685 rand a tonne from settlement 716 rand. Yellow maize was bid at 700 rand and offered at 750 rand from a 610 rand close.
Le Clus said forward contracting of maize on the physical market had also increased.

Official estimates put South Africa's 1996/97 commercial maize crop at 9.48 million tonnes. Le Clus said the former black homeland areas, which are calculated separately, contributed 444,000 tonnes taking the total crop to 9.93 million.
